title: App and CLI together
description: Take a preset exported from the app into a project with kikx apply, see how it differs from kikx setup, and re-run it safely.
outcomes: Know what a preset exported from the app contains
Vendor a preset into an existing project with kikx apply
Choose between kikx setup and kikx apply
Re-run a command safely, and apply into a separate folder to compare
recap: A preset is one JSON file that lists the project settings and every component with its values.
kikx apply renders a preset into a folder of an existing project and leaves kikx.toml alone.
kikx setup starts a new project from a preset and refuses to run where kikx.toml already exists.
Both check every file before writing, so a refused run writes nothing at all.
Applying into a separate folder is a safe way to compare a preset with what you have.

steps.intro: Many people design a project in the app and keep it in a repo with the CLI. Let's carry one from one to the other.
steps.open: I open the {template} template, as if you had built this project yourself.
steps.export: Export takes the project out of the app.
steps.presetOption: Preset saves the whole project as one {presetFile} file. That's the one the CLI reads.
steps.exported: Let's say you downloaded it into your repo. Here it is, next to nothing else yet.
steps.presetFile: A preset is plain JSON, so you can read it, review it and commit it.
steps.presetJson: It holds the project settings and the list of components, each with the values you entered in the app.
steps.init: This repo already has a kikx project, so I start with kikx init.
steps.apply: Your turn. Vendor the preset into the {outputDir} folder: kikx apply {presetPath} {flagInto} {outputDir}.
steps.vendored: kikx rendered every component of the preset with the real engine and lists each file it wrote.
steps.applied: Same files as the app would give you in a zip, now in your project.
steps.setupTry: What about kikx setup with the same file?
steps.setupRefused: setup refuses: it creates a new project, and this one already has a kikx.toml.
steps.versus: So: setup to start a new project from a preset, apply to bring a preset into a project you already have. apply never changes kikx.toml.
steps.rerun: Now, what if you run the same apply again, say after editing the files?
steps.nothingWritten: kikx checks every file before writing anything. One file exists, so it stops and writes nothing, not even the files that don't exist yet.
steps.force: {flagForce} would overwrite them all. To compare instead, apply into a folder of its own.
steps.staging: Your turn. Apply the same preset into a new folder: kikx apply {presetPath} {flagInto} {staging}.
steps.stagingFolder: A fresh copy sits in {staging}. Compare it with {outputDir} using diff or your editor, then keep what you want.
steps.done: The app and the CLI share presets: design in one, vendor with the other, and re-run without fear of losing your edits.
steps.presetComponent: Each component names its reference in the registry, like you would pass to kikx add, then its name and values.
steps.tomlKept: apply wrote files only. kikx.toml is still the one kikx init created.
steps.tomlName: Same name, {project}, not the one stored in the preset.
steps.lsStaging: Both folders now hold the same files.
steps.diff: In your own terminal, diff with the recursive option between {outputDir} and {staging} shows every line you changed since the first apply.
